body: The shop shuts at four and the boy has been sent for bread, which is why he is on the hill road at ten to. He is eleven. The phone in his pocket only works properly at the top, by the water tank, where the town falls away and you can see the whole bay, and he knows this the way he knows where the dogs are. He gets there and something is already playing, halfway through, and he stops walking. He does not sit down. He stands holding the bread with the bag handles cutting into his fingers until the song finishes, and then he goes down the hill and it drops out, and that is fine, because he knows where it lives now.

Nobody in that story was measured. Something arrived at a particular place, and a person found out where the edge of it was by standing at the edge of it. That is what reach means before anybody turns it into a figure.

There is a map on this site, and what it shows is not a listener count. It shows where this band is aimed — which languages are carried, which regions have a station hosted in their own tongue, and where the dial is still silent.

That distinction is the whole argument, and the word reach is worth taking literally to see why. Reach is a verb before it is ever a noun. It describes an arm going out towards something that is not yet held. When it becomes a noun on a slide it stops describing anybody reaching anything at all — it describes a quantity of people who were briefly in the vicinity of a thing, which is not the same event and does not deserve the same word. A map of aim is a statement about intent that can be checked against reality. A reach figure is a statement about the past that cannot be checked by anybody who is not being asked to trust it.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 assigned frequencies, of which 46 are on air. 40 of them make up the international stretch, carrying 29 languages besides English. All of that is printed on this site rather than described.

Publishing assignments before they are built is a costly way to work, and it was chosen deliberately. It means every frequency that is not yet on air is visible as a debt, sitting there in the list with a number beside it, and anybody can count them. It means a station that turns out to be harder than expected cannot be quietly dropped and forgotten, because its number is already spoken for and the silence at that number is a matter of public record. The frequencies are the plan, written down where anybody can hold us to them. There is no second, private plan.

Almost nothing else in this field works that way now. The ordinary language of ministry reporting is impressions, engagement, decisions, reached — enormous figures, generously defined, produced by the same organisation that benefits from them being large, and audited by nobody. Nobody sets out to mislead. It is simply what happens when funding follows numbers and no one has agreed what the numbers mean. The cost lands on the reader, who ends up unable to tell an organisation doing serious work from one that is good at counting, and eventually stops trying to tell.

So the band is arranged the other way round. A frequency is assigned at the moment a station is decided on, not at the moment it is finished — the number comes first, then the build, then the air. Stations sit in their bands by kind, the ministry formats together, the international stretch together, the always-on formats together, so that a silent number is silent in an obvious place, surrounded by neighbours that are playing.
None of this means audience does not matter. It means that at this stage, honesty about audience runs out very quickly.

Be fair to the figures first. Knowing who is listening is genuinely useful; it tells you which language to build next and when a station is not working. But internet numbers are elastic in a way broadcast numbers never were. A stream opened for four seconds counts. A page loaded by a machine counts. And the deeper problem is not accuracy, it is what chasing the figure does to the programming: an organisation optimising for reach will always, quite reasonably, build the frequency with the most speakers behind it before the one with the fewest, and it will keep doing that forever, and the small languages will keep waiting forever, and every step of it will look like good stewardship.
A number you cannot check is not information. It is decoration.

A man of seventy in a flat in Bulgaria is being shown something on his daughter’s laptop, mostly to be polite. He spent thirty-one years at a transmitter site outside the city, first as a technician and then running it, and he has not talked about that for a long time because nobody asks. She is scrolling a list of frequencies. He stops her at HM 327.20 and reads the line twice, in his own language, on a band that did not exist when he retired. Then he asks her for a pen. He writes the number on the back of an envelope from the pile by the telephone, folds it once, and puts it in his coat pocket, where it stays.
He did not write down how many people were listening. He wrote down where the thing was, which is the only piece of information a broadcast band has ever really owed anybody.

What genuinely is not known here is who is listening, and where. This band is young, a good many of its frequencies are still in build, and any claim about audience size at this stage would be a guess wearing the clothes of a fact. Nor can it be promised that every assigned number will be on air by a particular date, because some of them depend on finding people who do not yet know they are needed. That is uncomfortable to publish and it is published anyway.

The discomfort is the mechanism, though, not a flaw in it. A plan that can embarrass you is the only kind that can be trusted, because it is the only kind that costs something to break. A private roadmap and a large impressive number can coexist happily for years without a single station going on air. A public list of numbers cannot: either the frequency is playing when you tune to it or it is not, and there is nothing to interpret and nobody to take your word for it.

So the honest version of where this band is going is a list, not a projection. The map shows the aim. The frequency list shows the commitments. The on-air stations show what has actually landed, and the gap between the last two is the work, visible as it happens rather than described afterwards. Anybody is welcome to keep score, and keeping score is not an inconvenience here. It is what the list is for.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial, and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there is the international stretch, each language on its own frequency with its own host rather than translated in afterwards. The map is worth a minute before you start, because it will tell you which of those are lit and which are still owed.

If you want somewhere to begin, begin at HM 312.10 — Island Hallelujah, Pacific Island worship, slack-key and ukulele and island reggae, hosted by Tahoma Inspire. Begin there because it is this whole article in one frequency. No plan built around audience size would ever have assigned a permanent number to the islands; they are a rounding error on any chart of speakers, and that is precisely why they were given one. Put it on and you are hearing what it sounds like when a band aims at a place rather than at a total. It is also, as it happens, very good, which is the sort of thing you only find out by tuning to a station you would not have selected.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have, including on a hill with one bar of signal. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So here is an invitation that is also a test. Put HM 312.10 on this afternoon, and then go and look at the frequency list and find a number that is assigned and silent. Write it down somewhere you will come across it again — the back of an envelope will do. Come back in a year and tune to it. Either there will be a station there or there will not, and you will not have to take anybody’s word for which. That is the only kind of promise worth printing.
